title: The Hat on the Chair
bigQuestion: Holmes says there is no crime in it, and then reads a whole man off a hat he has never seen worn. Watson calls it a waste of energy. Who is right — and what has the hat actually proved, as against what it has only suggested?

nocrime.title: “No crime” — only an intellectual problem
text: “The matter is a perfectly trivial one, but there are points in it that are interesting, and even instructive.”
“No, no. No crime,” said Sherlock Holmes, laughing.
“Only one of those whimsical little incidents that will happen when you have four million human beings all jostling each other within the space of a few square miles.”
“Do you know Peterson, the commissionaire?”
“No, no; he found it. Its owner is unknown.”
“Look upon it, not as a battered billycock, but as an intellectual problem.”

fled.title: Everybody runs, and Peterson is left holding the goose
text: “Peterson rushed forward to protect the stranger from his assailants, but the man, shocked at seeing an official-looking person in uniform rushing towards him, dropped his goose, took to his heels, and vanished amid the streets.”
“The thugs also fled at the appearance of Peterson, so that he was left in possession of the spoils of victory, this battered hat and a most impressive Christmas goose.”
“Which surely he restored to their owner?”
“There lies the problem.”

baker.title: A card on the goose, and initials in the hat
text: “It is true that ‘For Mrs. Henry Baker’ was printed upon a small card that was tied to the bird’s leg, and it is also true that the initials ‘H.B.’ are legible upon the lining of this hat; but, as there are thousands of Bakers and hundreds of Henry Bakers in this city, it is not easy to restore lost property to any one of them.”
“He brought both hat and goose to me on Christmas morning, knowing that even the smallest problems interest me.”
“The goose we retained until there were signs that it should be eaten without delay.”
“Peterson has carried it off therefore to fulfill the ultimate destiny of a goose, while I continue to retain the hat of the unknown gentleman who lost his Christmas dinner.”

reason.title: Seeing and reasoning are not the same thing
text: “I can see nothing,” said I, handing it back.
“On the contrary, Watson, you can see everything. You fail, however, to reason from what you see.”
“Then, pray tell me what you can infer from this hat?”
“It is perhaps less suggestive than it might have been, and yet there are a few inferences that are very distinct, and a few others that are at least probable.”

list1.title: The man Holmes describes without ever meeting him
text: “That the man was highly intellectual is of course obvious, and also that he was fairly well-to-do within the last three years, although he has now fallen upon evil days.”

“He had foresight, but has less now than formerly, pointing to a moral slip, which, when taken with the decline of his fortunes, seems to indicate some evil influence, probably drink, at work upon him.”
“This may account also for the obvious fact that his wife has ceased to love him.”
“My dear Holmes!”

list2.title: Sedentary, middle-aged, and no gas in the house
text: “He has, however, retained some degree of self-respect,” he continued.
“He leads a sedentary life, goes out little, is out of shape entirely, is middle-aged, has grizzled hair that he has had cut within the last few days, and which he anoints with lime-cream.”
“Also, by the way, it is extremely unlikely that he has gas in his house.”
“You are certainly joking, Holmes.”
“Not in the least.”

capacity.title: Holmes puts the hat on his own head
text: “For example, how did you deduce that this man was intellectual?”
As an answer, Holmes clapped the hat upon his head.
It settled on the bridge of his nose.
“It is a question of capacity,” said he. “A man with so large a brain must have something in it.”

threeyears.title: A three-year-old hat of the very best quality
text: “This hat is three years old. These flat brims curled at the edge came in fashion then.”
“It is a hat of the very best quality.”
“If this man could afford to buy so expensive a hat three years ago, and no hat since, then he has gone down in the world.”

securer.title: The hat-securer, and the ink over the stains
text: “Here is the foresight,” said he, putting his finger upon the little disc and loop of the hat-securer.
“They are never sold upon hats. If this man ordered one, it is a sign of foresight, since he went out of his way to take this precaution against the wind.”
“But since he has broken the elastic and has not troubled to replace it, it is obvious that he has less foresight now than formerly, which is a distinct proof of a weakening nature.”
“On the other hand, he has endeavored to conceal some of these stains upon the felt by daubing them with ink, which is a sign that he has not entirely lost his self-respect.”

brushed.title: A hat nobody has brushed for weeks
text: “But his wife – you said that she had ceased to love him.”
“This hat has not been brushed for weeks.”

“When I see you, my dear Watson, with a week’s accumulation of dust upon your hat, and when your wife allows you to go out in such a state, I shall fear that you also have been unfortunate enough to lose your wife’s affection.”

waste.title: “Rather a waste of energy”
text: “Well, it is very ingenious,” said I; “but since there has been no crime committed and no harm done except the loss of a goose, all this seems to be rather a waste of energy.”

burst.title: The door flies open
text: Sherlock Holmes had opened his mouth to reply, when the door flew open, and Peterson the commissionaire rushed in with the face of a man who is dazed with astonishment.
“See what my wife found in its throat!”

missions.name: Chapter 1 — pages 126 to 130
missions.blurb: A hat and a goose arrive at Baker Street, and Holmes says there is no crime in it

vs.q: Watson supposes the hat will lead to the solving of a mystery and the punishment of a crime. What does Holmes say?
opts: That the crime is a small one, and hardly worth pursuing
That there is no crime in it at all
That the crime will not be known for some days yet
That a crime has been committed but nobody has reported it
vs.why: “No, no. No crime,” said Sherlock Holmes, laughing. Remember that he says this, and remember when the door flies open at the end of the reading.

vs.q: What does Holmes call the business of the hat and the goose?
opts: A trifle beneath his notice
A case he has taken on for a fee
One of those whimsical little incidents of a crowded city
A puzzle sent to him by the police at Scotland Yard
vs.why: “Only one of those whimsical little incidents that will happen when you have four million human beings all jostling each other within the space of a few square miles.” Four million people bumping into each other: the city itself is what produces the problem.

vs.q: A billycock, as the reader’s glossary has it, is what?
opts: A walking stick with a curved handle
A man’s felt hat
A uniformed doorman or messenger
A card tied to a parcel
vs.why: A man’s felt hat. Holmes uses the word to put the object down and then picks it straight back up: not a battered billycock, but an intellectual problem — the same thing, looked at differently.

vs.q: “Look upon it, not as a battered billycock, but as an intellectual problem.” What is Holmes asking Watson to do?
opts: To find out who made the hat
To stop thinking about the goose
To treat a worthless object as worth reasoning about
To guess the owner’s name from the initials inside
vs.why: Nothing about the hat changes. What Holmes is asking Watson to change is his own attention — which is the whole argument of this chapter, and the thing Watson keeps failing to do.

vs.q: Holmes says there is no crime, and spends the morning on it anyway. What does that tell you about him?
opts: He has no other work at present
He takes on small problems to keep himself amused between real cases
A problem interests him because it is a problem, not because it is a crime
He is hoping a crime will turn up in it later
vs.why: He calls it trivial in the same breath as interesting and even instructive. Later in the reading Watson complains it is a waste of energy; by then Holmes has drawn a portrait of a stranger from a hat, which is exactly the return he was after.

hi: shocked at seeing an official-looking person in uniform
dropped his goose, took to his heels

vs.q: Why did the stranger run away from Peterson?
opts: He had recognised Peterson from somewhere
He took him for a policeman coming for him
He was afraid the thugs would follow him
He had no money to pay for the broken window
vs.why: “Shocked at seeing an official-looking person in uniform rushing towards him.” Peterson was running to help. A man who bolts from a uniform is a man who does not want to be asked questions — and he had just broken a window.

vs.q: What did the stranger leave behind him?
opts: His hat and his walking stick
The goose and the card tied to its leg
His hat and the goose
Nothing — he took the goose and dropped only his hat
vs.why: The hat had already been knocked off; then “dropped his goose, took to his heels.” Everything Holmes reasons from for the next five pages was left in the street by a man in a hurry.

vs.q: Holmes calls the hat and the goose “the spoils of victory.” Why is that phrase a joke?
opts: Peterson had not fought anybody for them
The goose was not worth very much
Peterson had to give them both back at once
The hat was too battered to be worth keeping
vs.why: Everyone ran — the stranger and the thugs alike — and Peterson was left standing in the street with a hat and a goose he did not want. He won a battle nobody fought.

vs.q: Watson asks whether Peterson restored the hat and goose to their owner. What is Holmes’s answer?
opts: That the owner refused to take them back
That there lies the problem
That Peterson could not be troubled to try
That he advertised for the owner and got no reply
vs.why: “There lies the problem.” An honest man cannot return lost property to a man he cannot name — and finding the name is the intellectual problem Holmes has set himself.

vs.q: Three people run away in this scene. What does the story get out of that?
opts: It shows how dangerous the streets were at night
It leaves an honest man holding clues nobody claims
It shows that Peterson was braver than the others
It explains why the police were never called
vs.why: If the stranger had stayed, there would be no story: he would have picked up his hat and gone home. The whole case exists because the only person who did not run was the one person with no interest in any of it.

hi: thousands of Bakers and hundreds of Henry Bakers

vs.q: What was printed on the card tied to the goose’s leg?
opts: “For Mrs. Henry Baker”
“H.B., Tottenham Court Road”
“A Merry Christmas from H.B.”
“For Mr. Henry Baker, with thanks”
vs.why: For Mrs. Henry Baker — his wife, not himself. Holmes uses that card twice: once to explain why the goose cannot be returned, and once to prove the man is not a bachelor.

vs.q: What is written inside the hat?
opts: A maker’s name and a London address
The initials “H.B.”
The single word “Baker”
Nothing at all that can be read
vs.why: The initials H.B., legible on the lining. Two clues that agree with each other — and together they are still not enough to find one man.

vs.q: Why can Holmes not simply return the property to Henry Baker?
opts: Because the card gives no address to send it to
Because the initials in the hat might belong to anyone
Because there are hundreds of Henry Bakers in London
Because Peterson has already eaten the goose
vs.why: “Thousands of Bakers and hundreds of Henry Bakers in this city.” A name is not an identification in a city of four million — which is why the hat, and not the card, is the interesting object.

vs.q: What became of the goose?
opts: It is still waiting at Baker Street for its owner
Peterson took it home to be eaten before it spoiled
It was given away to a neighbour on Christmas Day
Holmes sent it back to the shop it came from
vs.why: “The goose we retained until there were signs that it should be eaten without delay.” A small practical detail, and the story turns on it: Mrs. Peterson is about to prepare that bird.

vs.q: Holmes keeps the hat and lets the goose go. What does that choice say about how he works?
opts: The goose was of no value to anybody
He expected the owner to come back for the hat
A worn object carries more about its owner than a new one
He had already learned all that he could from the goose
vs.why: A goose is a goose. A hat has been worn by one man for three years and has taken the marks of everything he has done in that time — so it is the hat he keeps, and the hat that fills the next four pages.

missions.name: Chapter 2 — pages 131 to 132
missions.blurb: Watson looks at the hat, sees everything, and reads nothing

hi: You fail, however, to reason from what you see
a few inferences that are very distinct

vs.q: What does Watson say when he hands the hat back?
opts: That he can see nothing
That he can see only the initials
That the hat tells him its owner was poor
That he would rather hear Holmes’s conclusions
vs.why: “I can see nothing,” said I, handing it back — immediately after describing the hat in eleven separate particulars. He does not realise he has just read out the answer.

vs.q: What is Holmes’s reply, and what does it mean?
opts: That Watson is not looking closely enough
That Watson needs the lens to see properly
That Watson sees everything but does not reason from it
That there is genuinely nothing at all there to see
vs.why: “On the contrary, Watson, you can see everything. You fail, however, to reason from what you see.” It is the sentence the whole story is built on, and it is a compliment and a correction at once.

vs.q: What is the difference Holmes is pointing at?
opts: Between looking at a thing and looking for a thing
Between seeing a thing and working out what it means
Between using a lens and using the naked eye
Between guessing at a thing and proving it
vs.why: Observation and inference are two separate jobs. Watson is good at the first and does not attempt the second; Holmes does both and only the second one looks like magic.

vs.q: How careful is Holmes about how certain his conclusions are?
opts: He presents every one of them as proved
He says the hat can prove almost nothing
He separates the distinct inferences from the merely probable
He refuses to say anything at all until Watson has tried
vs.why: “A few inferences that are very distinct, and a few others that are at least probable.” He grades his own conclusions before he gives them. Notice which ones he later hedges: the drink, and the wife.

vs.q: Holmes says the hat is “less suggestive than it might have been.” Why say so before starting?
opts: To lower what Watson expects of him
Because he has not finished examining it
Because the hat has been handled by far too many people
Because the evidence is honestly thinner than he would like
vs.why: It would be easy to oversell the hat, and he does the opposite. A man who tells you the evidence is not as good as it might be is a man worth believing about what it does show.

hi: his wife has ceased to love him

vs.q: What does Holmes say is “of course obvious” about the man?
opts: That he is a Londoner
That he is highly intellectual
That he is out of work
That he is no longer young
vs.why: Highly intellectual — and the reason turns out to be a great deal funnier and simpler than the word suggests. Hold the question until page 133.

vs.q: What does Holmes say about the man’s money?
opts: That he has never had very much of it
That he was well-to-do three years ago and has since fallen on evil days
That he has come into money in the last three years
That he has always spent everything he earns on keeping up appearances
vs.why: Well-to-do within the last three years, now fallen upon evil days. Two facts in one sentence: he had money, and he has lost it. The hat supplies both.

vs.q: What does Holmes think is at work on the man, and how sure is he?
opts: Illness, and he is certain of it
Some evil influence, probably drink — probable, not certain
Gambling, which he says the hat proves outright
Nothing at all — the man has simply been rather unlucky
vs.why: “Some evil influence, probably drink, at work upon him.” Probably. This is one of the guesses he warned Watson about, reached from a declining fortune and a slipping character together.

vs.q: What does Holmes say about the man’s wife, and how does Watson react?
opts: That she has left him; Watson agrees at once
That she has ceased to love him; Watson protests
That she is dead; Watson asks how he knows
That she manages the household money; Watson says nothing
vs.why: “The obvious fact that his wife has ceased to love him.” “My dear Holmes!” Watson’s protest is the reader’s: that is not the sort of thing a hat can possibly tell you. Two pages later it does.

vs.q: Holmes has never met this man. What is remarkable about the list he gives?
opts: It is all about the man’s appearance
It is all guesswork and he admits as much
It describes the man’s mind, money and marriage from an object
It contradicts what Peterson had actually seen in the street
vs.why: Brains, money, character, marriage — a whole life, from a hat found in the road. Whether you believe it depends entirely on the next two pages, which is exactly where the story puts them.

hi: unlikely that he has gas in his house

vs.q: What good thing does Holmes still say about the man?
opts: That he has kept some degree of self-respect
That he is generous with what little he has
That he has never been in trouble with the police
That he is kind to his wife despite everything
vs.why: “He has, however, retained some degree of self-respect.” The word however is doing the work: after the drink and the marriage, Holmes goes out of his way to find something creditable in the man.

vs.q: How does Holmes describe the way the man lives?
opts: A hard worker, out in all weathers
A traveller, rarely at home
A sedentary life, going out little and out of shape entirely
A restless man who can never manage to sit still for long
vs.why: Sedentary, goes out little, out of shape entirely. Notice that this comes from the same hat as the man’s intellect — a hat that has spent most of its life hanging up indoors.

vs.q: What does Holmes say about the man’s hair?
opts: That it is thinning at the crown
That he wears it long and untidy
That it is grizzled, recently cut, and dressed with lime-cream
That it has been dyed in order to hide the grey coming through
vs.why: Grizzled, cut within the last few days, anointed with lime-cream. Three separate facts about a man’s head, from the lower part of a lining — and he explains all three on page 134.

vs.q: What is the last thing on Holmes’s list, and why is it the strangest?
opts: That the man is middle-aged, which anyone might guess
That the man has no gas in his house, which is not about him at all
That the man goes out very little, which the dust had already shown
That the man has grizzled hair, which the lining showed
vs.why: “It is extremely unlikely that he has gas in his house.” Everything else on the list is about the man; this is about his staircase. Holmes throws it in as an afterthought — “also, by the way” — and it is the one Watson cannot let pass.

vs.q: “You are certainly joking, Holmes.” “Not in the least.” What does this exchange set up?
opts: An argument the two of them never settle
Holmes proving each conclusion in turn
Watson going off to find Henry Baker himself
Holmes admitting that he has gone too far
vs.why: Watson has stopped believing, so Holmes stops asserting and starts explaining. Everything in the next two pages is an answer to this one line of doubt, taken in the order Watson asks for it.

missions.name: Chapter 3 — pages 133 to 134
missions.blurb: Holmes shows his work: the brim, the securer, the lining and the dust

hi: clapped the hat upon his head

vs.q: How does Holmes prove the man is intellectual?
opts: By the careful way the hat has been mended
By the quality of the hat he chose to buy
By putting the hat on his own head
By the books listed in the papers beside him
vs.why: He claps it on and it settles on the bridge of his nose. No lens, no reasoning — he simply tries the hat on, and it is far too big for him.

vs.q: “It is a question of capacity.” What does Holmes mean by capacity here?
opts: How much the man could afford to spend on a hat
How much the hat can hold — the size of the head
How much the man is able to remember
How well the hat has stood up to wear
vs.why: Capacity as in volume. “A man with so large a brain must have something in it.” The joke is that he is measuring a mind with a hat, and saying so with a completely straight face.

vs.q: Is this a good piece of reasoning?
opts: Yes — head size is a reliable measure of intelligence
No — a big hat only proves a big head
Yes — because Holmes is never wrong about people
No — because the hat may not be the man’s own
vs.why: It is the weakest link in the chain and the story is not hiding it: Victorians believed a large skull meant a large intellect, and it does not. Holmes calls it “of course obvious,” which is what people say when they have not checked.

vs.q: Why does the hat settling on the bridge of Holmes’s nose make the point so quickly?
opts: It shows that Holmes has a small head
It shows the hat was made for somebody else entirely
It shows the hat is far too large for a normal head
It shows the hat has lost its shape with age
vs.why: Watson does not have to be told; he can see it. It is the one deduction in the chapter that is demonstrated rather than argued, which is why Holmes leads with it.

vs.q: Of all the conclusions on Holmes’s list, which does this one rest on the least evidence?
opts: This one — the size of the hat and nothing more
The decline of his fortunes — the age of the hat
The lime-cream — the smell of the lining
The candle — the wax stains on the felt
vs.why: The wax, the dust, the hair ends and the securer are all marks left by things the man actually did. The size of his head is just the size of his head, and everything else Holmes builds on it is guesswork.

hi: This hat is three years old
flat brims curled at the edge

vs.q: How does Holmes know the hat is three years old?
opts: A date is stamped inside the lining
Its flat brim curled at the edge was the fashion three years ago
Three years of dust have gathered in it
The maker went out of business three years ago, as he recalls
vs.why: “These flat brims curled at the edge came in fashion then.” He is dating an object by its style, the way you might date a photograph by the clothes in it.

vs.q: What does Holmes say about the quality of the hat?
opts: That it was cheap when new
That it was of the very best quality
That it was made to order rather than bought
That it was good but not the best to be had
vs.why: The very best quality. That is what makes the age of it mean something: an expensive hat, three years old, and nothing bought since.

vs.q: Which two facts, put together, tell Holmes the man has come down in the world?
opts: The broken elastic and the ink stains
The dust indoors and the marks of moisture
An expensive hat, three years old, and no hat since
The red silk lining and the missing maker’s name
vs.why: Either fact on its own says nothing. A man may buy a fine hat and keep it; a man may own one old hat and never have had money. Only both together show a fall.

vs.q: Suppose the hat had been cheap and three years old. What could Holmes have concluded?
opts: That the man had grown poorer still
That the man had come up in the world
Nothing about his fortunes either way
That the man cared nothing for his appearance
vs.why: A poor man with an old cheap hat is just a poor man. The deduction needs the gap between what he once could afford and what he has now, and a cheap hat leaves no gap to measure.

vs.q: Watson calls this one “clear enough, certainly.” Why does he accept it so readily?
opts: Because Holmes has proved it with the lens
Because it follows from two things he can check himself
Because he had already thought of it himself
Because it is the least surprising thing on the list
vs.why: He can feel the quality of the felt and he can be told the fashion. Compare the wife and the gas, which he fights every step of the way — Watson believes what he can verify.

hi: the little disc and loop of the hat-securer
a distinct proof of a weakening nature

vs.q: What is a hat securer, and what is it for?
opts: A band inside the hat to make it fit better
A disc and loop with an elastic, to stop the hat blowing away
A stiffener sewn into the brim to hold the hat in its shape
A pin that fastens the hat to the hair
vs.why: A little disc and loop with an elastic — “this precaution against the wind.” Holmes puts his finger on it and calls it the foresight, which is a lot to call a piece of elastic.

vs.q: Why does the hat securer prove foresight?
opts: Because hats are never sold with one, so he ordered it specially
Because it was expensive to have fitted
Because only a careful man would wear a hat in windy weather
Because it had to be sewn on by the man himself
vs.why: “They are never sold upon hats. If this man ordered one, it is a sign of foresight, since he went out of his way to take this precaution.” Somebody had to ask for it: that is the whole argument.

vs.q: What does Holmes read into the broken elastic that was never replaced?
opts: That the man lost the hat some time ago
That the man has grown careless about his own appearance now
That he has less foresight than he had, and a weakening nature
That somebody else has been wearing the hat
vs.why: The same small object twice over: ordering it showed foresight, not mending it shows the foresight going. “A distinct proof of a weakening nature.” Holmes gets a change over time out of a thing that does not move.

vs.q: What does the ink daubed over the stains tell Holmes?
opts: That the man had no money for a new hat
That the man works with ink and got it on the felt
That he minds how he looks, so keeps some self-respect
That he tried to hide the hat’s age from his wife
vs.why: “Which is a sign that he has not entirely lost his self-respect.” A man daubing ink on a stained hat is a man still hoping to look respectable, and it is the one point where Holmes gives him credit.

vs.q: The securer and the ink point in opposite directions. What does Holmes do about that?
opts: He decides the ink is the more reliable of the two
He treats the contradiction as proof the hat had two owners
He keeps both: a man slipping who has not given up
He drops the securer and relies on the ink
vs.why: “On the other hand” — he does not tidy the evidence into one story. The elastic says he is letting himself go; the ink says he is still trying. Holding both is what makes Henry Baker a person instead of a conclusion.

missions.name: Chapter 4 — pages 135 to 136
missions.blurb: The wife, the candle, “a waste of energy” — and the door flies open

hi: has not been brushed for weeks
a week’s accumulation of dust upon your hat

vs.q: What is the evidence that the man’s wife has stopped loving him?
opts: The card addressed to her rather than to him
The hat has not been brushed for weeks
The state of the lining and the hair cream
That he was out alone at four in the morning
vs.why: An unbrushed hat. That is the whole of it — and Holmes told Watson at the start that some of his inferences were only probable. This is the boldest one in the story.

vs.q: What is the assumption hiding inside that deduction?
opts: That a man never brushes his own hat
That a wife would let her husband go out dusty only if she no longer cared
That the man cannot afford to have the hat properly cleaned and brushed
That the hat had been hanging up for weeks unworn
vs.why: Holmes needs it to be a wife’s business to brush her husband’s hat. In 1890 that assumption passed without comment; today the reasoning is the most dated thing in the story, and worth noticing as such.

vs.q: How does Holmes make the point to Watson?
opts: By reminding him of an earlier case
By pointing out the dust with the lens
By joking that a dusty hat on Watson would mean the same thing
By asking Watson when his own hat was last brushed at home
vs.why: “When I see you, my dear Watson, with a week’s accumulation of dust upon your hat… I shall fear that you also have been unfortunate enough to lose your wife’s affection.” He uses Watson’s own marriage as the worked example.

vs.q: What does that joke tell you about the two men’s friendship?
opts: That Holmes is careless of Watson’s feelings
That Watson’s marriage is a sore subject between them
That Holmes can tease him about his private life
That Holmes envies Watson for being married
vs.why: You can only make that joke to a close friend. Notice too what it assumes: that Watson’s hat is brushed, and that Holmes has noticed.

vs.q: Is this the strongest or the weakest of Holmes’s conclusions?
opts: The strongest — he calls it an obvious fact
Among the weakest — an unbrushed hat has many explanations
The strongest — nothing else explains the dust
Among the weakest — because the man may not be married
vs.why: He calls it “the obvious fact,” which is a good deal more confident than the evidence deserves. The man might live alone, or be ill, or have a wife with troubles of her own — and the story has Watson push back at once.

hi: no crime committed and no harm done except the loss of a goose

vs.q: What is Watson’s verdict on the whole performance?
opts: That Holmes has proved his case completely
That it is ingenious, but rather a waste of energy
That Holmes has guessed too much from too little
That they should go and look for Henry Baker at once
vs.why: “Well, it is very ingenious,” said I; “but… all this seems to be rather a waste of energy.” He is convinced by the reasoning and unconvinced that it was worth doing, which are two different things.

vs.q: What is Watson’s reason for calling it a waste?
opts: Henry Baker will never be found in a city that size
The goose has already been eaten
No crime has been committed and nobody has been harmed
Holmes has no client and will not be paid
vs.why: “No crime committed and no harm done except the loss of a goose.” It is exactly what Holmes himself said at the start of the reading — Watson is agreeing with him and complaining at the same time.

vs.q: Holmes said the same thing five pages earlier. Why does it sound different now?
opts: Because Holmes has changed his mind since
Because Holmes meant it as a reason to look and Watson as a reason not to
Because Watson has proved there was no crime
Because the goose has been eaten in the meantime and cannot be examined
vs.why: “No crime” was Holmes’s invitation: a problem worth having for its own sake. In Watson’s mouth the same words mean there was nothing here to bother with. The two of them value the work differently.

vs.q: Who has the better of this argument, on the evidence so far in the reading?
opts: Holmes — he has read a stranger’s life off a hat
Watson — nothing has come of it but a portrait nobody can use
Neither — both are right about different things
Holmes — because the hat will lead him to Henry Baker
vs.why: Holmes has done something remarkable; Watson is right that it has changed nothing. Both positions stand up — which is why the story puts the interruption exactly here.

vs.q: Why does the story give Watson the last word before the interruption?
opts: To show that Watson is usually right
To make Holmes look foolish for once
To set up the worst possible moment to be proved wrong
To bring the chapter to a close on a quieter note
vs.why: Watson says it is all a waste of energy. Holmes opens his mouth to reply and does not get a word out, because the door flies open. The timing is the joke.

hi: had opened his mouth to reply

vs.q: What happens as Holmes is about to answer Watson?
opts: Peterson sends a message round to Baker Street
The door flies open and Peterson rushes in
Henry Baker himself knocks at the door
A telegram arrives from the police
vs.why: “Sherlock Holmes had opened his mouth to reply, when the door flew open.” He is interrupted mid-argument, and the interruption settles the argument better than any reply could.

vs.q: How does Peterson look when he comes in?
opts: Frightened, as though he had been followed
Angry about the goose he was given
Like a man dazed with astonishment
Out of breath from running all the way
vs.why: “With the face of a man who is dazed with astonishment.” Not frightened, not hurt — astonished. Whatever has happened is a surprise rather than a disaster, and the reading stops there.

vs.q: Who found the thing Peterson has come about?
opts: Peterson himself, as he prepared the bird
Holmes, before he sent the goose away
Peterson’s wife
Mrs. Henry Baker, who claimed the goose
vs.why: The picture on page 136 has it: “See what my wife found in its throat!” The goose went home to be eaten, and the person cooking it is the person who found something.

vs.q: Where was it found?
opts: In the throat of the goose
Tied to the card on the bird’s leg
Sewn into the lining of the hat
In the street where the hat was dropped
vs.why: In the goose’s throat. Tonight’s reading stops before you are told what it is — which is the point at which a chapter ending earns its keep.

vs.q: Peterson bursting in the instant Watson says “no crime” is a trick of the storyteller. What is it for?
opts: To show that Peterson is an unreliable witness
To hide the fact that Holmes had no answer ready
To turn a hat nobody wanted into the start of a case
To remind the reader that the goose had been eaten
vs.why: For five pages this has been an exercise about an old hat, with both men agreeing there is no crime in it. One opened door turns all of that reasoning into the opening of something much larger — and every word of it still counts.

title: The Stone in the Goose
bigQuestion: A stone worth a fortune comes out of a goose, and a plumber is already going to trial for stealing it. Holmes says he cannot tell whether that man is innocent, but he is certain about Henry Baker. What made the difference?

stone.title: What Peterson’s wife found
text: “See here, sir! See what my wife found in its throat!”
He held out his hand and displayed on his palm a brilliant blue stone.
It was smaller than a bean in size, but of such purity and radiance that it twinkled like an electric point.
“A diamond, sir! A precious stone!”
“It’s more than a precious stone. It’s the precious stone.”
“Not the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle?” I blurted.

worth.title: A thousand pounds, and not a twentieth of the price
text: “I ought to know its size and shape, seeing that I have read about it in The Times every day lately.”
“It is absolutely unique, and its value can only be guessed at, but the reward offered of a thousand pounds is certainly not within a twentieth part of the market price.”
“A thousand pounds! Great Lord of mercy!”
The commissionaire plumped down into a chair and stared from one to the other of us.
“And I have reason to know that there are sentimental considerations that would induce the Countess to part with half her fortune if she could recover the gem.”

accused.title: Lost five days ago, and a plumber under arrest
text: “It was lost, if I remember correctly, at the Hotel Cosmopolitan,” I remarked.
“Precisely so, just five days ago.”
“John Horner, a plumber, was accused of having taken it from the lady’s jewel case.”
“The evidence against him was so strong that the case has been referred to the Superior Court.”
John Horner, 26, plumber, was brought up upon the charge of having stolen from the jewel case of the Countess of Morcar the valuable gem known as the blue carbuncle.

ryder.title: The only person who says what happened in that room
text: James Ryder, upper attendant at the hotel, testified that he had shown Horner up to the dressing room of the Countess of Morcar upon the day of the robbery, in order that he might solder the grate, which was loose.
He had remained with Horner a little while, but had finally been called away.
On returning he found that Horner had disappeared, that the bureau had been forced open, and that the small casket in which the Countess kept her jewel was lying empty on the table.
Ryder instantly gave the alarm, and Horner was arrested the same evening; but the stone could not be found.

court.title: What the police court made of it
text: Catherine Cusack, maid to the Countess, testified to hearing Ryder’s cry of dismay on discovering the robbery, and to having rushed into the room, where she found matters were as described by Ryder.
Inspector Bradstreet gave evidence as to the arrest of Horner, who struggled frantically, and protested his innocence.
Evidence of a previous conviction for robbery having been given against the prisoner, the magistrate refused to deal with the offense, but referred it to the Superior Court.
Horner, who had shown intense emotion during the proceedings, fainted away at the conclusion, and was carried out of court.

chain.title: From a jewel case at one end to a goose’s throat at the other
text: “Hum! So much for the police court,” said Holmes thoughtfully, tossing aside his paper.
“The question for us now to solve is the sequence of events leading from a burglarized jewel case at one end to the throat of a goose at the other.”
“Watson, our little deductions have suddenly assumed a less innocent aspect.”
“Here is the stone; the stone came from the goose, and the goose came from Mr. Henry Baker, the gentleman with the bad hat and all the other characteristics with which I bored you.”
“So now we must set ourselves very seriously to finding this gentleman.”

advert.title: The simplest means first
text: “To do this, we must try the simplest means first – an advertisement in all the evening papers.”
“Found at the corner of Goodge Street, a goose and a black felt hat. Mr. Henry Baker can have them back by visiting at six-thirty this evening at 221b Baker Street.”
“Very. But will he see it?”
“Well, he is sure to keep an eye on the papers, since, to a poor man, the loss was a heavy one.”
“And, Peterson, buy a goose on your way back and leave it here. We must have one to give to this gentleman in place of the one your family is devouring.”

devil.title: “They are the devil’s baits”
text: “Of course it is a focus of crime. Every good stone is. They are the devil’s baits.”
“This stone is not yet twenty years old. It was found in China, and it is remarkable in having every characteristic of the carbuncle, except that it is blue, instead of ruby red.”
“It has already a sinister history. There have been two murders, a suicide, and several robberies brought about for the sake of this blue carbuncle.”
“I’ll lock it up in my strongbox and drop a line to the Countess to say that we have it.”

innocent.title: “I cannot tell”
text: “Do you think this man Horner is innocent?”
“I cannot tell.”
“Do you imagine that this other one, Henry Baker, had anything to do with the matter?”
“It is, I think, more likely that Henry Baker is an absolutely innocent man, who had no idea that the bird he was carrying was of more value than if it were made of gold.”
“That, however, I shall determine by a very simple test, if we have an answer to our advertisement.”

baker.title: Henry Baker at last
text: As I approached the house I saw a tall man in a soft woolen cap, with a coat that was buttoned up to his chin, waiting outside.
He was a large man, with rounded shoulders, a massive head, and a broad, intelligent face with a grizzled brown beard.
His rusty black coat was buttoned up in front and his wrists protruded from his sleeves.
He spoke in a choppy fashion, choosing his words, and gave the impression of a man of learning who had had a run of bad luck.
“Money has not been so plentiful with me as it once was,” he remarked.
“I had no doubt that the thugs who assaulted me had carried off both my hat and the bird. I did not care to spend more money in a hopeless attempt at recovering them.”

test.title: The very simple test
text: “By the way, about the bird – we were compelled to eat it.”
“To eat it!” Our visitor half rose from his chair in his excitement.
“But I presume that this other goose on the sideboard, which is about the same weight and fresh, will answer your purpose equally well?”
“Oh certainly, certainly!” answered Mr. Baker, with a sigh of relief.
“Of course, we still have the feathers, legs, throat, and so on of your bird, if you wish –”
“They might be useful to me as relics of my adventure,” said he, “but, no, sir, I think that, with your permission, I will confine my attentions to the excellent bird that I see upon the sideboard.”
Sherlock Holmes glanced sharply across at me with a slight shrug of his shoulders.

club.title: The goose club at the Alpha Inn
text: “By the way, would you tell me where you got the other one from? I am a fowl fancier, and I have seldom seen a better-grown goose.”
“There are a few of us who frequent the Alpha Inn near the museum.”
“This year our good host, Windigate by name, instituted a goose club, by which, for a few pence every week, we were to receive a bird for Christmas.”
“My pence were duly paid, and the rest is familiar to you.”
“So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes. “It is certain that he knows nothing whatever about the matter.”
“Then I suggest that we turn our dinner into a supper and follow this clue while it is still hot.”

missions.name: Section 1 — pages 137 to 138
missions.blurb: What Peterson’s wife found in the goose, and what it is worth

hi: smaller than a bean in size

vs.q: What does Peterson bring to Baker Street, and where did it come from?
opts: A card from the goose’s leg, found by his wife
A blue stone, found in the goose’s throat
A ring, found in the pocket of the hat
A letter, found pushed under his door
vs.why: His wife found it while preparing the bird. The goose Holmes gave away to be eaten turns out to have been carrying the thing the whole story is about.

vs.q: How does the reader describe the stone itself?
opts: As large and heavy, about the size of a walnut and dull
As dull until it was cleaned
As smaller than a bean, twinkling like an electric point
As a deep ruby red, cut into facets
vs.why: “Smaller than a bean in size, but of such purity and radiance that it twinkled like an electric point.” An electric point was a new and startling kind of brightness in 1890 — the comparison is doing real work.

vs.q: Peterson says, “A diamond, sir! A precious stone!” What does Holmes correct him with?
opts: That it is coloured glass, and worth nothing at all
That it is a ruby rather than a diamond
That it is not a diamond but a carbuncle
That it is not a precious stone but the precious stone
vs.why: “It’s more than a precious stone. It’s the precious stone.” One word of difference, and it turns a lucky find into the thing every newspaper in London has been writing about.

vs.q: Who names the stone, and what does that tell you about him?
opts: Watson — he has been following the case in the papers
Holmes — he had recognised it at once by its shape
Peterson — his wife had read about it
Nobody — Holmes has to send for a jeweller
vs.why: “Not the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle?” I blurted. Watson gets there first, out loud, and is right. He is a better detective than he was given credit for two pages earlier.

vs.q: Five pages ago Holmes said there was no crime in this business. What has changed?
opts: Nothing — losing a goose is still not a crime
A stranger has turned out to be a thief
The object of a famous robbery has turned up in the evidence
Peterson has admitted that he kept the bird on purpose
vs.why: The hat and the goose were a puzzle about an unknown gentleman. One stone on a commissionaire’s palm turns the same facts into evidence in a robbery with a man already awaiting trial.

hi: not within a twentieth part of the market price
read about it in The Times

vs.q: What reward has been offered for the stone?
opts: A hundred pounds
A thousand pounds
Half the Countess’s fortune
No reward has been offered at all
vs.why: A thousand pounds — and Holmes points out at once that it is “not within a twentieth part of the market price,” so the stone is worth more than twenty thousand. In 1890 that is a fortune.

vs.q: What does Holmes say about the reward compared with what the stone is worth?
opts: The reward is more than the stone could ever fetch
The reward is about what the stone is worth
The reward is less than a twentieth of its value
Nobody can say, because it has never been valued
vs.why: Which tells you something about the Countess as well as the stone: she is offering a very large sum and still getting a bargain, because no honest buyer could be found for a stolen carbuncle anyway.

vs.q: How does Holmes come to know the stone’s size and shape without having seen it?
opts: He had read about it in The Times every day lately
He had been consulted by the Countess herself
He had seen it in a jeweller’s window in London
Inspector Bradstreet had described it to him
vs.why: He has read about it in the paper every day. The crumpled newspapers beside his couch on the first page of the story turn out not to be idleness.

vs.q: Besides money, what reason does Holmes give for the Countess wanting the stone back?
opts: She needs it to settle a debt
She has promised it to a museum
There are sentimental considerations
She means to sell it and leave England
vs.why: “Sentimental considerations that would induce the Countess to part with half her fortune if she could recover the gem.” The stone matters to her for a reason that has nothing to do with its price.

vs.q: How does Peterson react to the figure of a thousand pounds?
opts: He asks Holmes whether he may claim it
He drops into a chair and stares at them
He laughs and says it cannot be true
He offers to take the stone to the police himself
vs.why: “Great Lord of mercy!” and he plumps down into a chair. He is an honest man who has just been told that the bird he took home was carrying a year’s wages many times over.

vs.q: Where and when was the carbuncle lost?
opts: At the Alpha Inn, on Christmas morning
At the Hotel Cosmopolitan, five days ago
At the Countess’s own house, a week ago
In Goodge Street, on the night of the row
vs.why: The Hotel Cosmopolitan, five days before. Count forward: the robbery, then Christmas morning in Tottenham Court Road, then the second morning after Christmas in Baker Street. The dates matter.

vs.q: Who has been accused of the robbery?
opts: James Ryder, an attendant at the hotel
Catherine Cusack, the Countess’s maid
Henry Baker, who lost the goose
John Horner, a plumber
vs.why: John Horner, 26, a plumber, who had been working in the Countess’s dressing room that day. Hold on to the fact that he is a workman called in, and the only person in the room who did not belong to the hotel.

vs.q: How far has the case against Horner already gone?
opts: He has been questioned and released
He has been charged, but has not yet been arrested at all
The evidence was strong enough to send it to the Superior Court
He has already been tried and sentenced
vs.why: The magistrate would not deal with it himself and referred it on. Which means a trial is coming, and the clock is running on whatever Holmes is going to do about it.

vs.q: What does Holmes do when Watson mentions the Hotel Cosmopolitan?
opts: Sends out for the morning’s papers
Writes at once to Inspector Bradstreet
Finds the newspaper report among his own papers
Says he has heard nothing at all about the case
vs.why: He rummages among the papers he has been lying in all morning until he finds the paragraph, and reads it out. Everything he needs is already in the room.

vs.q: Why does it matter that a man is already awaiting trial for this robbery?
opts: It means the police will not listen to Holmes
It means that the stone must have been stolen twice over
It means Holmes’s puzzle now has somebody’s freedom in it
It means the Countess will withdraw her reward
vs.why: The hat was an exercise. Now the same chain of facts leads to a man in a cell who fainted in court, and the question of whether he put the stone where it was found.

missions.name: Section 2 — pages 138 to 140
missions.blurb: The newspaper’s account of the robbery, and the chain Holmes sees in it

hi: James Ryder, upper attendant at the hotel
solder the grate, which was loose

vs.q: Why was Horner in the Countess’s dressing room at all?
opts: He had been sent up with a message
He had been shown up to solder a loose grate
He was there to clean the chimney
He had come to the hotel to deliver the jewel case
vs.why: A plumber, shown up to mend a loose grate. He had a reason to be in the room and somebody else put him there — which is a strange way to begin a robbery.

vs.q: Who showed Horner up to the room?
opts: Catherine Cusack, the Countess’s maid
The Countess of Morcar herself
James Ryder, the upper attendant
Nobody — he went up on his own
vs.why: James Ryder, upper attendant at the hotel. Notice how much of this story is Ryder’s: he takes Horner up, he is the one who leaves, he is the one who comes back, and he is the one who raises the alarm.

vs.q: According to Ryder, what happened while he was out of the room?
opts: Horner disappeared, the bureau was forced, the casket left empty
Horner finished the grate and went away quietly
The Countess came in and took the jewel herself
Cusack found Horner standing at the bureau, and called out
vs.why: That is Ryder’s account of it. Read it again as what it is — testimony — rather than as what happened, because the only person who says the room was emptied while he was away is the person who was away.

vs.q: Who raised the alarm?
opts: Horner, when he found the casket empty
Ryder, the moment he came back
Catherine Cusack, from the passage
The Countess, on returning to dress
vs.why: “Ryder instantly gave the alarm.” Instantly. He is quick, and he is helpful, and everything the police know about the robbery begins with him.

vs.q: Horner was arrested that same evening. What was never found?
opts: The tools he had been working with
The casket the jewel had been kept in
The stone
The grate he had been sent up to mend
vs.why: “But the stone could not be found.” A man is going to trial for taking a stone nobody could find on him — and it turns up days later in a goose’s throat on the other side of London.

hi: struggled frantically, and protested his innocence

vs.q: What does Catherine Cusack’s evidence actually add?
opts: That she saw Horner at the bureau
That she heard Ryder’s cry and found things as he described
That the Countess had shown her the jewel that morning
That Horner had asked her about the jewel case
vs.why: Read it carefully: she heard Ryder shout, and she arrived to find matters as Ryder described. She is a witness to Ryder’s discovery, not to the robbery. Nobody saw the stone taken.

vs.q: How did Horner behave when he was arrested?
opts: He confessed at once and asked for mercy
He went quietly, saying nothing at all
He struggled frantically and protested his innocence
He ran for it, and had to be caught in the street outside
vs.why: Inspector Bradstreet’s evidence. A man fighting and shouting that he is innocent looks guilty to a court, and looks exactly the same whether he is or not.

vs.q: What piece of evidence weighed heaviest against Horner?
opts: That he was found with hotel property on him
That he could not say where he had gone
That he had been convicted of robbery before
That Ryder had seen him open the bureau
vs.why: “Evidence of a previous conviction for robbery.” It is why the magistrate sent the case up. Notice that it is not evidence about this robbery at all — it is evidence about who he is.

vs.q: How did Horner take the proceedings?
opts: He showed no feeling throughout
He laughed at the magistrate
He showed intense emotion and fainted at the end
He asked to give evidence himself and was refused
vs.why: “Fainted away at the conclusion, and was carried out of court.” The reader is given this and then nothing more about him for pages, which is part of what makes the case urgent.

vs.q: Three people gave evidence. What does none of it establish?
opts: That the stone was missing from the casket
That Horner had been in the room
That Horner was ever seen taking the stone
That Ryder had left the room for a time
vs.why: The casket was empty, Horner had been there and was gone, Ryder shouted and Cusack came running. Not one witness describes the theft. The whole case is what people found afterwards.

hi: So much for the police court
a burglarized jewel case at one end to the throat of a goose at the other
the goose came from Mr. Henry Baker

vs.q: How does Holmes describe the problem now in front of them?
opts: Deciding whether Horner is guilty or not
Returning the stone to the Countess as quickly as possible
The sequence of events from a jewel case to a goose’s throat
Finding out which of the hotel servants could have been bribed
vs.why: It is a beautiful way to put a problem: two ends that are known, and the whole middle missing. Everything he does for the rest of the story is filling in that middle.

vs.q: What does Holmes mean by “our little deductions have suddenly assumed a less innocent aspect”?
opts: That he no longer trusts what the hat told him
That the hat reasoning was a waste of time after all
That the same conclusions now bear on a crime
That Watson was right to call it a waste of energy
vs.why: Nothing he worked out about the hat has changed or been withdrawn. What has changed is what it is for: a portrait of a shabby gentleman is now a description of a man the police will want to talk to.

vs.q: What is the chain Holmes lays out, in order?
opts: Baker, then the goose, then the stone, then the hotel
The stone came from the goose, the goose from Henry Baker
The hotel, then Horner, then Peterson, then the hat
The goose came from the hotel, and the stone from Horner
vs.why: He works backwards from what he is holding: stone, goose, Baker. That is why finding Baker is the next job and not, say, going to the hotel — Baker is the nearest unknown link.

vs.q: What does Holmes decide to do first?
opts: Call on the Countess of Morcar
Visit Horner in his cell
Go down to the Hotel Cosmopolitan himself
Set himself seriously to finding Henry Baker
vs.why: “So now we must set ourselves very seriously to finding this gentleman.” Very seriously — the same man whose hat was a morning’s amusement is now the only lead there is.

vs.q: Why is Henry Baker the right person to look for next, rather than anyone at the hotel?
opts: The police are already working on the hotel
He is the last person known to have had the goose
He is the only suspect Holmes has
He lives nearer to Baker Street than the others
vs.why: The chain is broken between the hotel and the goose, and Baker is standing at the near end of the gap. Work from what you have towards what you do not — and nobody has suggested Baker is a suspect.

missions.name: Section 3 — pages 140 to 142
missions.blurb: The advertisement, the stone’s history, and who might be innocent

hi: to a poor man, the loss was a heavy one

vs.q: What is the “simplest means” Holmes tries first?
opts: Calling at every hat shop in London
An advertisement in all the evening papers
Asking the police to circulate a description
Waiting for Baker to come and ask for the hat
vs.why: An advertisement. Before anything clever, the obvious thing — and it works, which is why he tried it first.

vs.q: What does the advertisement offer, and where?
opts: A reward for news of a goose and a hat
A goose and a black felt hat, back at 221b Baker Street
The return of a lost hat, at the Alpha Inn
A thousand pounds for the stone, at Scotland Yard
vs.why: “Found at the corner of Goodge Street, a goose and a black felt hat… at six-thirty this evening at 221b Baker Street.” Notice what it does not say: nothing about a stone, and nothing about the police.

vs.q: Watson asks whether Baker will even see the advertisement. Why is Holmes sure he will?
opts: Baker is a man of learning who reads everything
The advertisement is to appear in every paper in London
To a poor man, losing a Christmas goose is a heavy loss
Baker lives close enough to see it posted in the street
vs.why: He is reasoning from the man, not from the newspaper. A poor man who has lost his Christmas dinner will be watching the papers — which is the same reasoning he did off the hat, used forwards.

vs.q: What errand does Holmes add for Peterson besides the advertisement?
opts: To fetch Inspector Bradstreet to Baker Street
To buy another goose and leave it there
To say nothing to his wife about the stone
To take the stone to the Countess at once
vs.why: “We must have one to give to this gentleman in place of the one your family is devouring.” A small courtesy — and the second goose turns out to be the whole of the test he sets Baker.

vs.q: The advertisement mentions Goodge Street but not the stone. Why would Holmes leave that out?
opts: Because the stone is not Baker’s to be given back
Because the police had asked him to keep it quiet
Because a guilty man would be warned off by it
Because the Countess had not yet been told it was found
vs.why: If Baker put the stone in the goose, an advertisement naming it is a warning to stay away. Mentioning only a hat and a bird is what makes the invitation safe to accept — and makes who turns up worth knowing.

hi: two murders, a suicide, and several robberies

vs.q: What does Holmes call every good stone?
opts: A fortune waiting for an owner
A focus of crime, and the devil’s baits
A thing more trouble than it is worth
The one honest form of money
vs.why: “Of course it is a focus of crime. Every good stone is. They are the devil’s baits.” Not this stone in particular — all of them. It is a remark about people rather than about jewels.

vs.q: What makes this stone unusual as a carbuncle?
opts: It is larger than any other known
It was cut in China rather than in Europe
It is blue instead of ruby red
It is older than any other in England
vs.why: “Every characteristic of the carbuncle, except that it is blue, instead of ruby red.” That is where the story gets its title, and why the stone cannot be sold or mistaken for another.

vs.q: What history does the stone already have?
opts: It has been lost and found three times before
It has passed through six owners in twenty years
Two murders, a suicide and several robberies
It was taken from a temple and never recovered
vs.why: And it is not twenty years old. Holmes lays this out immediately after calling it the devil’s baits — the sinister history is his evidence for the remark, not decoration.

vs.q: What does Holmes do with the stone, and what does he do about the Countess?
opts: Sends it to her at once by a messenger
Locks it in his strongbox and writes to her
Gives it to Peterson to take to the police
Keeps it in his pocket until the case is done
vs.why: Strongbox, and a line to say that they have it. He does not hand it over, because he still needs the goose it came out of to lead somewhere — but he will not leave her wondering either.

vs.q: Why does Holmes talk about the stone’s history at all, just here?
opts: To explain why it is worth so much money
To show why it cannot be sold openly
To explain why he intends to keep it safely locked up
To say what such a stone does to the people near it
vs.why: He has a man in a cell, a stranger with a bad hat, and a robbery nobody saw. The remark about the devil’s baits is him saying what kind of story this is likely to turn out to be.

hi: more value than if it were made of gold

vs.q: Watson asks whether Horner is innocent. What does Holmes answer?
opts: That he is certainly innocent
That he is almost certainly guilty
That he cannot tell
That the court has already decided the matter
vs.why: “I cannot tell.” Three words, and they are the most honest thing he says all evening. He has a stone and a goose and no idea yet how they met.

vs.q: What does Holmes think about Henry Baker’s part in it?
opts: That he is more likely an absolutely innocent man
That he is the thief and the goose was his hiding place
That he was paid by somebody else to carry the bird
That he cannot say until he has seen the man
vs.why: More likely innocent — a man with no idea “that the bird he was carrying was of more value than if it were made of gold.” A guess, offered as a guess, and he says how he means to check it.

vs.q: How does Holmes say he will settle the question of Baker?
opts: By questioning him closely about the goose
By asking Bradstreet to look into his record
By a very simple test
By watching the house to see who comes with him
vs.why: “A very simple test, if we have an answer to our advertisement.” Simple is the word to notice — what he actually does is offer the man a different goose and watch his face.

vs.q: Holmes will not guess about Horner but will guess about Baker. What is the difference?
opts: Baker has not been accused of anything
He has a way to check the guess about Baker
Horner has a previous conviction against him
Baker is a poor man and Horner is not
vs.why: A guess you can test is worth making; a guess you cannot is just an opinion. He has no way to test Horner, so he says “I cannot tell” and leaves it.

vs.q: Watson says he will come back in the evening. What does that say about the state of the case?
opts: Holmes has sent him away so he can work alone
Holmes expects to have solved it by then
There is nothing to be done until Baker answers
Watson has lost interest in the business
vs.why: “And you can do nothing until then?” “Nothing.” The whole investigation is waiting on one advertisement and one stranger choosing to turn up.

missions.name: Section 4 — pages 143 to 146
missions.blurb: Henry Baker himself, the very simple test, and the goose club

hi: a man of learning who had had a run of bad luck
Money has not been so plentiful with me as it once was
a hopeless attempt at recovering them

vs.q: What is Henry Baker like when he finally appears?
opts: A small nervous man who will not sit down
A large man with a massive head and a grizzled beard
A young man, well dressed and confident
An elderly man who can hardly walk without help
vs.why: Large, round-shouldered, massive head, broad intelligent face, grizzled brown beard. Hold it against the hat: a big head, greying hair, middle-aged. Holmes had him right.

vs.q: Which of Holmes’s conclusions does Baker’s appearance bear out?
opts: That he keeps no servant in the house
That his wife has ceased to love him
That he is out of shape entirely and goes out little
That he had money three years ago and has none now
vs.why: A rusty black coat buttoned to the chin, wrists out of the sleeves, and “the impression of a man of learning who had had a run of bad luck.” The decline Holmes read off the brim is standing in the room.

vs.q: Why had Baker never advertised for his lost hat and goose?
opts: He had not realised they were missing
He thought the thugs had taken them, and could not afford to try
He was ashamed of having broken the window
He had been too ill to go out of doors since Christmas Day
vs.why: “Money has not been so plentiful with me as it once was… I did not care to spend more money in a hopeless attempt at recovering them.” An advertisement costs money he has not got.

vs.q: What does Baker’s reason for not advertising confirm?
opts: That he had something to hide about the bird
That he had come down in the world
That he had not been in London at Christmas
That he blamed Peterson for taking them
vs.why: He gives it with “a rather shamefaced laugh,” which is the detail that makes it true. Nobody pretends to be too poor to place an advertisement.

vs.q: How does the way Baker speaks fit what Holmes said about him?
opts: He speaks roughly, so Holmes was wrong about his learning
He says almost nothing, so nothing can be told
He chooses his words, like an educated man fallen on hard times
He talks too much, which Holmes had not predicted
vs.why: “He spoke in a choppy fashion, choosing his words.” Holmes said highly intellectual on the strength of a hat size, which was bad reasoning — and he still turns out to have been right, which is a different thing from being right for a good reason.

vs.q: What does Holmes tell Baker about his goose?
opts: That it is waiting for him downstairs
That it had to be given away to a neighbour
That they were compelled to eat it
That it had spoiled and was thrown out
vs.why: He says it straight out and then watches. The whole test is in what Baker does in the next few seconds.

vs.q: How does Baker react when he hears the bird has been eaten?
opts: He half rises from his chair in excitement
He says it does not matter in the least
He asks whether anything was found inside it
He accuses Holmes of having stolen it
vs.why: “To eat it!” Half out of his chair — and then entirely satisfied the moment another goose is offered. A man who knew what was in that bird would not be calmed by a fresh one.

vs.q: What does Holmes offer him besides the fresh goose?
opts: The feathers, legs and throat of the first bird
The thousand pounds of reward the stone would earn
A hat to replace the battered one
Payment for the bird that was eaten
vs.why: “The feathers, legs, throat, and so on of your bird.” Throat. Holmes puts the one part of the goose that matters in front of him, and Baker laughs it off as a relic.

vs.q: What is Baker’s answer to that offer, and what does it prove?
opts: He takes the remains, which shows he is looking for something
He takes both, which shows nothing either way
He refuses them and takes the fresh bird, so he knows nothing
He asks to be left alone with them, which makes Holmes suspicious
vs.why: He would rather have the good goose on the sideboard than the giblets of his own. Anybody who had hidden a stone in that throat would have taken the remains without hesitating.

vs.q: Holmes glances at Watson with a shrug. What is he saying?
opts: That he does not believe a word of it
That Baker is not the man they want
That Watson should keep quiet about the stone
That the test has failed and must be tried again
vs.why: The test is over and it is settled. No question was asked and no accusation made — Baker was offered two things and chose the one an innocent man would choose.

vs.q: How does Holmes get Baker to say where the goose came from?
opts: By telling him the bird may have been stolen
By offering him money for the information
By asking as one fowl fancier admiring a fine bird
By asking him directly where he had bought it
vs.why: “I am a fowl fancier, and I have seldom seen a better-grown goose.” A compliment, not a question — and Baker answers it happily on his way out of the door.

vs.q: Where did Baker get his goose?
opts: He bought it at a market on Christmas Eve
From a goose club at the Alpha Inn
It was a gift from his landlord
From a shop near the museum, on Christmas Eve
vs.why: A goose club run by Windigate, the host of the Alpha Inn: a few pence every week through the year and a bird at Christmas. That is how a poor man comes by a Christmas goose.

vs.q: What is Holmes’s verdict on Henry Baker?
opts: That he is hiding something after all
That he may be worth watching for a while
That he knows nothing whatever about the matter
That he should be questioned again tomorrow
vs.why: “So much for Mr. Henry Baker. It is certain that he knows nothing whatever about the matter.” Certain — a word he refused to use about Horner, and uses here because he has tested it.

vs.q: What does Holmes decide to do instead of having dinner?
opts: Write up his notes on the case so far
Go to the police with what he has found
Wait at Baker Street for news of Horner’s trial
Turn dinner into supper and follow the clue at once
vs.why: A bitter night, coats and scarves, and a quarter of an hour later they are at the Alpha Inn. He will not let the trail cool for the sake of a meal.

vs.q: At the end of the reading, what has the investigation actually gained?
opts: The name of the thief who took the stone
A link from the stone back to where the goose came from
Proof that John Horner is innocent
The reward of a thousand pounds from the Countess
vs.why: One more link, and no more: stone, goose, Baker, and now the place Baker got the bird. Horner is still in a cell and nobody knows who put the stone in the goose.
